blocks.text: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the baby clinic for a routine check. At birth he weighed 3.4 kg, on the 50th centile. Today the nurse plots 7.2 kg, which sits on the 9th centile line. His mother says he is a happy baby who feeds well, but he is not yet sitting without support. One plotted point and one developmental observation: are these two findings linked, and which one worries you more?

blocks.markdown:
Growth and development are the two outcome measures of childhood health. **Growth** is the increase in size (weight, length or height, head circumference). **Development** is the acquisition of skills in several domains. Both are measured against reference populations, and in both the *trajectory over time* matters more than a single value.

**Growth charts.** In the UK, the **UK-WHO** charts are used: the WHO standard describes the growth of healthy, mostly breastfed infants from birth to 4 years, and UK 1990 data are used for older children and for the preterm range. A **centile** tells you the percentage of the reference population at or below a given measurement: a child on the 25th centile is larger than 25% of children of the same age and sex. The principal centile lines on UK-WHO charts are 0.4th, 2nd, 9th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 91st, 98th and 99.6th, and the **gap between two neighbouring lines is a 'centile space'**. A healthy child tends to track along one centile. Plot weight, length or height, and head circumference at each check, and use **corrected age** for infants born before 37 weeks until at least 2 years.

blocks.title: Faltering growth
blocks.text: Faltering growth (previously called failure to thrive) is a slower rate of weight gain than expected, shown by a weight that falls across centile lines. UK guidance (NICE) suggests concern when weight falls across one or more centile spaces if birth weight was below the 9th centile, two or more if birth weight was between the 9th and 91st centiles, and three or more if birth weight was above the 91st centile. A weight below the 2nd centile or a very low rate of gain also warrants assessment.

blocks.markdown:
**Why growth falters.** The principle is energy balance: weight gain requires intake to exceed losses and expenditure. Causes fall into **inadequate intake** (the commonest: feeding difficulty, insufficient milk, poor technique, neglect or poverty), **malabsorption or excessive losses** (coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic diarrhoea, vomiting or reflux) and **increased requirements** (chronic infection, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, hyperthyroidism), as well as endocrine and genetic causes (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome). A good history, feeding history, family heights, examination and targeted tests identify the group. Always consider neglect.

**Z-scores and target height.** A **z-score** (standard deviation score) states how many standard deviations a measurement lies from the reference mean. A **mid-parental height** predicts expected adult height range.

blocks.caption: x is the child's measurement, mu the reference mean (or median) and sigma the reference standard deviation. A z of 0 is the 50th centile, about -2 the 2nd centile and about +2 the 98th. Parental heights H are in centimetres; the 13 cm is the average adult male-female difference.

blocks.title: Converting a measurement to a z-score
blocks.prompt: A 4-year-old girl weighs 14.0 kg. In the reference data used (illustrative values) the mean weight for girls of her age is 16.6 kg with a standard deviation of 1.8 kg. Calculate her z-score and say which centile it approximates.

steps.text: Subtract the mean from the measurement.

Interpret: a z-score of about -1.4 lies between -1 (about the 16th centile) and -2 (about the 2nd centile), so she is around the 9th centile. This is on the lower range of normal; the trend over time matters more than this single value.

blocks.answer: z is about -1.4, approximately the 9th centile, which is a low but not unusual value; repeat measurements show whether she is tracking or falling.

blocks.markdown:
**Development.** Development proceeds in a predictable order from head to toe and from proximal to distal, and the domains are **gross motor, fine motor and vision, speech and language, and social, emotional and self-care**. Milestones have a range of normal: what matters is the **pattern** and whether the child has *lost* skills.

For infants born preterm, assess against **corrected age** (chronological age minus the number of weeks born early) until about 2 years. For example, a child who is 40 weeks old, born at 30 weeks, is 10 weeks early and should be assessed at about 30 weeks' corrected age.

blocks.caption: Selected typical milestones (averages; individual children vary within a range).
rows: Reaches and grasps, transfers between hands
Pulls to stand, cruises; walks alone between about 12 and 15 months
Feeds with a spoon, points to show interest
Runs, kicks a ball, climbs stairs
Alternates feet on stairs, pedals tricycle
Copies a circle, tower of about 9 cubes
Short sentences of 3 or more words
Plays with other children, dresses with help

blocks.title: Using corrected age
blocks.prompt: A girl born at 32 weeks' gestation (term is 40 weeks) is now 14 months old chronologically and is not yet walking, although she pulls to stand. Is this delayed?

steps.text: Calculate how early she was born: 40 minus 32 equals 8 weeks, which is about 2 months.
Calculate corrected age: 14 months minus 2 months equals 12 months.

Compare with milestones at 12 months: pulling to stand and cruising are expected, walking independently is normal between about 12 and 15 months. She is performing at or above what is expected for her corrected age.

blocks.answer: Her corrected age is 12 months. Not yet walking is within normal limits and she is not developmentally delayed; she should be reviewed again as she approaches 18 months corrected.

items: No social smile by about 8 weeks, or not fixing and following.
Not sitting unsupported by about 9 to 10 months.
Hand preference before 12 months (suggests weakness on the other side).
No single words with meaning by 18 months, or no babble by 12 months; any concern about hearing.
Loss of any previously acquired skill at any age (regression).
Persistent parental concern, and abnormal tone or movement, or poor social engagement.

blocks.title: Red flags prompt referral
blocks.text: Developmental red flags (delay in one or more domains beyond the range of normal, regression, abnormal tone, or parental concern) should lead to referral for developmental assessment, including hearing and vision tests, and sometimes genetic and metabolic investigations. Regression is the most urgent flag. Always check hearing in a child with delayed speech.

points: Plot weight, length or height and head circumference on UK-WHO charts; use corrected age for preterm infants until about 2 years, and judge trajectory across centile spaces rather than a single point.

Faltering growth is weight falling across centile spaces (one or more if birth weight below the 9th centile, two or more if 9th to 91st, three or more if above the 91st); causes are inadequate intake, malabsorption or losses, and increased requirements.
A z-score is (measurement minus mean) divided by standard deviation; z of -2 is about the 2nd centile. Mid-parental height uses the sum of parents' heights plus or minus 13 cm, halved.
Development is assessed in gross motor, fine motor and vision, speech and language, and social domains with a range of normal for each milestone.
Red flags include regression, no sitting by 9 to 10 months, no walking by 18 months, no words by 18 months, early hand preference and parental concern; refer with hearing and vision assessment.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old girl had a birth weight on the 75th centile. At the 6-month check she was on the 50th centile and now she is on the 25th centile. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Her weight has fallen across two centile spaces, which meets the criterion for faltering growth and needs assessment
She is tracking normally because she is above the 2nd centile
She is normal because the 9th centile is within the normal range
A fall across centile lines is only significant if she drops below the 0.4th centile

questions.correctOptionText: Her weight has fallen across two centile spaces, which meets the criterion for faltering growth and needs assessment

distractorRationale.a: From the 75th to the 25th centile crosses two centile spaces (75th to 50th, and 50th to 25th) in a child with birth weight between the 9th and 91st centiles, which is the threshold for concern.
distractorRationale.b: Being above the 2nd centile does not make a falling trajectory normal.
distractorRationale.c: The value itself is within the normal range, but the fall from her own trajectory is the concern.
distractorRationale.d: The criterion is based on the fall across centile spaces, not a fixed cut-off.

questions.explanation: A healthy child tends to track along one centile, so a fall across two or more centile spaces from a birth weight between the 9th and 91st centiles meets the criterion for faltering growth. The trend, not an absolute cut-off, triggers assessment for inadequate intake, malabsorption or increased requirements.

questions.stem: At what age is a social smile typically first seen in a healthy term infant?

options.text: 6 to 8 weeks
6 months
12 months
At birth

distractorRationale.a: The social smile in response to a face appears at about 6 to 8 weeks.
distractorRationale.b: By 6 months an infant laughs and rolls, so this is much too late.
distractorRationale.c: By 12 months the child waves and plays peek-a-boo.
distractorRationale.d: Newborns show reflex smiles but not a responsive social smile.

questions.explanation: The social smile is one of the first social milestones, appearing at about 6 to 8 weeks. Its absence by about 8 weeks is a red flag that prompts assessment of vision, hearing and development.

questions.stem: Which combination of skills would be typical of a healthy 2-year-old?

options.text: Runs, builds a tower of about 6 cubes and joins two words together
Hops on one foot, copies a triangle and speaks in long sentences
Crawls, has a neat pincer grip and says mama and dada non-specifically
Rolls over, laughs and turns to a voice

questions.correctOptionText: Runs, builds a tower of about 6 cubes and joins two words together

distractorRationale.a: Running, a tower of about 6 cubes and two-word phrases are typical at 2 years.
distractorRationale.b: Hopping, copying a triangle and long sentences are skills of 4 to 5 year olds.

questions.explanation: By 2 years a child runs, builds a tower of about 6 cubes and begins to join two words. The other options describe infants of 6 and 9 months or children of 4 to 5 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following should prompt urgent referral for developmental assessment?

options.text: A 20-month-old who used to say several words and has now stopped speaking and avoids eye contact
A 6-month-old who is not yet crawling
A 13-month-old who is pulling to stand but not yet walking alone
A 3-month-old who is not yet rolling over

questions.correctOptionText: A 20-month-old who used to say several words and has now stopped speaking and avoids eye contact

distractorRationale.a: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) at any age is a red flag.
distractorRationale.b: Most infants do not crawl at 6 months.
distractorRationale.c: Walking alone is normal between about 12 and 15 months, and pulling to stand is expected.
distractorRationale.d: Rolling is not expected at 3 months.

questions.explanation: Regression of language and social skills is the most important developmental red flag at any age and needs prompt assessment. The other three children are showing milestones within the normal range of timing.

questions.stem: A boy was born at 28 weeks' gestation (term is 40 weeks) and is now 15 months old chronologically. He sits well and cruises but is not yet walking alone, and says one or two words. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: His corrected age is about 12 months, so his development is appropriate and no referral is needed on this basis
He is delayed because he is not walking at 15 months
Corrected age should not be used after the first birthday
He should be referred urgently for regression

questions.correctOptionText: His corrected age is about 12 months, so his development is appropriate and no referral is needed on this basis

distractorRationale.a: He was 12 weeks (about 3 months) early, so corrected age is about 12 months; sitting, cruising and a couple of words are expected then.
distractorRationale.b: Judged on chronological age he would appear delayed, but corrected age is the right reference.
distractorRationale.c: Corrected age is used until about 2 years.
distractorRationale.d: There is no loss of skills.

questions.explanation: Born 12 weeks early, he is about 3 months younger developmentally, so his corrected age is about 12 months and his skills fit this age. Correction is used until about 2 years, so judging him by chronological age would wrongly label him as delayed.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is 90.0 cm tall. In the reference data used (illustrative values) the mean height for boys his age is 96.0 cm with a standard deviation of 3.0 cm. Calculate his height z-score (a dimensionless number).
questions.explanation: The z-score is (90.0 minus 96.0) divided by 3.0, which is minus 6.0 divided by 3.0, or minus 2.0. A z-score of about minus 2 corresponds to about the 2nd centile, so he is at the lower edge of the reference range and needs a growth review and consideration of parental heights.

questions.stem: A girl's father is 178 cm tall and her mother is 162 cm tall. Using the mid-parental height formula for girls (father's height plus mother's height minus 13, all divided by 2), calculate her mid-parental height in centimetres.
questions.explanation: The sum of the parents' heights is 178 + 162 = 340 cm; subtracting 13 gives 327 cm, and halving gives 163.5 cm. This is a predicted adult height, with a normal range of about 8 to 10 cm either side, and helps decide whether short stature is familial.

questions.stem: A girl was born at 30 weeks' gestation (term is 40 weeks) and is now 52 weeks old chronologically. Calculate her corrected age in weeks.
questions.explanation: She was born 40 minus 30, which is 10 weeks early. Her corrected age is 52 minus 10, which is 42 weeks, so her development should be compared with that of a 42-week-old infant.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old boy was born at 3.5 kg and now weighs 8.1 kg, a fall from the 50th to below the 2nd centile. Discuss how you would assess him for faltering growth: the likely mechanisms, key history and examination points, and first-line approach.
markingGuide: Confirm accurate measurements, plot on UK-WHO chart and review the trajectory across centiles
Recognise energy balance: inadequate intake is the commonest cause, then malabsorption or losses, then increased requirements
History: feeding (type, volume, technique, timing of solids), vomiting, stool pattern, recurrent infection, family heights, social circumstances
Examination: general appearance, signs of chronic disease (heart murmur, clubbing, respiratory signs), dysmorphism, head circumference and length
Investigations guided by findings (for example urine, coeliac serology, sweat test, thyroid function)
First-line management: feeding assessment, dietitian input and weight monitoring; escalate if serious concern
questions.explanation: Faltering growth is a sign rather than a diagnosis, and the approach is to define the mechanism by history and examination. Most cases are due to inadequate intake and improve with feeding support, with investigation reserved for specific clues.

questions.stem: A mother is worried that her 22-month-old son has no words and does not point or respond when his name is called. Outline how you would assess this child and which findings would lead you to refer for developmental assessment.
markingGuide: Take a full developmental history across all four domains, including whether any skills have been lost
Birth and family history, hearing concerns and recurrent ear infections
Test hearing early because delayed speech may be due to hearing loss
Examine growth, head circumference, dysmorphic features, neurological signs and social engagement
Red flags present: no words by 18 months, poor response to name and no pointing, social communication difficulty
Refer for developmental (and audiology) assessment, since this exceeds the normal range
Take parental concern seriously and provide interim advice and follow-up
questions.explanation: At 22 months a child should have several words and joint attention behaviours, so the absence of words and poor response to name are outside the normal range. Hearing assessment is essential and referral for developmental assessment should be made without waiting.
